To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
IL-17A+ cells are present in the skin of patients with SSc, and their number is increased compared with normal skin and inversely correlated with skin involvement.

1) IL-17A+ cells are increased in systemic SSc skin and their numbers correlate with disease duration and severity, 2) IL-17+ cells are increased at the dermal-epidermal junction and in the dermis, and 3) the IL-17+ cell infiltrates are composed of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and γδ T cells.
IL-17A+ cells are increased in the lesional skin of patients with SSc.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and characterization of new, highly active and selective inhibitors of IL-17A.
the development of a new method for the detection of the presence of the interleukin-17 (IL-17) cytokine.
the study of the role of interleukin 17 (IL-17) in the pathogenesis of systemic sclerosis (SSc).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IL-17 is a key player in the pathogenesis of SSc and is a potential target for therapeutic intervention.
IL-17A and IL-17F are both important in the pathogenesis of psoriatic arthritis.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the number of Th17 cells in the skin correlates with the extent of disease activity in SSc.

the number of IL-17A+ cells in the skin of patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc) is increased, and this is associated with an increase in the number of IL1A, IL1B, IL1R1, IL6, and IL6R transcripts in skin fibroblasts and with the severity of skin involvement in SSc.

the number of IL-17A+ cells is increased in SSc skin and that this increase is inversely correlated to the extent of skin sclerosis, suggesting a role for IL-17 in the control of SSc disease activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
IL-17A+ cells are a significant contributor to the skin pathology of SSc and that they are associated with the extent of disease.
